name: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V)

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive myopathy caused by deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase, PYGM gene), impairing glycogen breakdown in skeletal muscle
Presents with exercise intolerance, painful muscle cramps, and early fatigue during brief high-intensity or sustained exertion
The classic 'second wind' phenomenon is a hallmark: symptoms ease if exercise is paused and then continued at a lower intensity as blood-borne fuels take over
Recurrent rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria (pigmenturia) can occur after strenuous activity and may precipitate acute kidney injury
The non-ischaemic (or ischaemic) forearm exercise test shows a flat or blunted rise in venous lactate with an exaggerated rise in ammonia
Serum creatine kinase is often persistently elevated at rest and rises further with exertion
Management is largely non-pharmacological: avoiding intense exertion, aerobic conditioning, and pre-exercise carbohydrate to reduce symptoms and rhabdomyolysis risk
reference.pathophysiology: McArdle disease is caused by deficiency of myophosphorylase, the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase encoded by PYGM, which initiates glycogen breakdown by cleaving glucose units from glycogen in skeletal muscle. Without functional enzyme, muscle cannot mobilise its glycogen stores to fuel anaerobic and early aerobic exercise, so ATP generation fails during intense or sustained activity, producing cramps, contractures, and fatigue. Because glycolysis downstream cannot be fed from glycogen, blood lactate does not rise normally with exercise. Energy-depleted muscle fibres are prone to injury and breakdown, causing rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria. The 'second wind' reflects the delayed availability of blood glucose and free fatty acids as alternative fuels once the circulation delivers them to working muscle.
additionalDifferentials: Other muscle glycogenoses (e.g. Tarui disease, phosphorylase b kinase deficiency)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders (e.g. CPT II deficiency)
Inflammatory or metabolic myopathies with rhabdomyolysis
additionalInvestigations: Forearm exercise test showing blunted lactate rise with exaggerated ammonia rise
Urine myoglobin testing after episodes of exertion
Molecular genetic testing of the PYGM gene
Muscle biopsy with histochemical staining for myophosphorylase activity
Renal function monitoring during episodes of rhabdomyolysis
redFlags: Severe rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine kinase and pigmenturia
Acute kidney injury following an episode of myoglobinuria
Fixed muscle contractures or severe cramps during exertion
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually normal and most patients remain functional with lifestyle adaptation; the principal risks are recurrent rhabdomyolysis and consequent acute kidney injury, and a minority develop fixed muscle weakness with age.
pitfalls: Dismissing exertional symptoms as deconditioning and missing the diagnosis for years
Performing an ischaemic forearm test with a tourniquet when a non-ischaemic protocol is safer and adequate
Advising complete avoidance of activity rather than encouraging graded aerobic conditioning
Overlooking the risk of acute kidney injury during rhabdomyolysis
references: Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
